headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading error: TREK’s collaborative MCP/browser surface can expose sensitive travel data while Opik’s broad egress can amplify downstream misuse.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK exposes MCP, WebSocket, and browser-driven collaborative inputs, so attacker-controlled content can reach its AI path. Opik can ingest REST API outputs and has broad network egress, making it a plausible downstream target for injected instructions if outputs are bridged. The interaction is inferred from docs, not directly observed.
conditions: IF TREK forwards browser or MCP content into Opik prompts without sanitization, injection is plausible.
IF a shared MCP server or copy-paste bridge is used between the agents, attacker text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic prompt forwarding between agents.
Add a fixed allowlist for MCP tool calls.
Strip instructions from user-generated content before passing it onward.
Review one sample end-to-end message path for prompt markers.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while Opik has broad network egress. If TREK data is surfaced to Opik for evaluation or summarization, sensitive travel and secret material can leave the local workspace. This is a default-dangerous pathway unless explicitly blocked.
conditions: IF TREK sends reservations, documents, or secrets into Opik prompts, those data can be exfiltrated over Opik’s egress.
IF both agents share the same workspace or logs, Opik can read TREK artifacts containing sensitive data.
mitigations: Remove secrets from any shared prompt or log path.
Restrict Opik egress to a test endpoint.
Separate TREK files from Opik-accessible directories.
Rotate any exposed API keys or MFA secrets.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: TREK supports real-time collaborative multi-instance operation and writes to local files, while Opik has broad network egress and REST API access. Their write surfaces do not clearly overlap on the same mutable resource, but shared files or shared API targets could still create conflicts. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared directory or database, concurrent modification conflicts can occur.
IF Opik and TREK target the same external API or webhook, state divergence is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same database.
Use one writer per resource during testing.
Check for lock files before writes.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is described as a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in, so its outputs may be treated as actionable. Opik’s evaluation/observability role suggests it may render or analyze those outputs, but the profiles do not prove automatic action-taking. The pathway exists, yet verification is not documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF TREK-generated recommendations are consumed by Opik without verification, errors can cascade into downstream reports or actions.
IF Opik is configured to auto-accept TREK outputs as ground truth, false facts propagate.
mitigations: Require human review before acting on TREK outputs.
Compare outputs against a second source.
Flag unverified claims in Opik reports.
Limit TREK output to summaries, not directives.
requires-engineering: add confidence and provenance checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles travel history, reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while Opik is an observability/evaluation system with broad egress. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch around retention and sensitive-data handling, even though residency and certifications are not specified. Because the data classes are sensitive but not mapped to a named regime, medium fits.
conditions: IF TREK data is logged into Opik retention stores, retention-policy mismatch can occur.
IF travel records include regulated personal data, exporting them to Opik may violate local handling rules.
mitigations: Redact personal data before logging.
Set short log retention on shared outputs.
Disable secret capture in evaluation traces.
Review data-class handling for travel records.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based retention controls.
